title: United Kingdom, Key Stages 2 and 3
subject: other-countries
year_note: Key Stages 2 and 3 are ages 7 to 14 in England. The NZ year band is a rough equivalent by age, not a curriculum match.

questions.prompt: How many nations make up the United Kingdom?
questions.explanation: The United Kingdom is made up of four nations: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of England?
questions.explanation: London is the capital of both England and the whole United Kingdom.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Scotland?
questions.explanation: Edinburgh is Scotland's capital, though Glasgow is Scotland's biggest city.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Wales?
questions.explanation: Cardiff, on the south coast of Wales, has been the Welsh capital since 1955.

questions.prompt: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
questions.explanation: Belfast, on the east coast, is the capital and largest city of Northern Ireland.

questions.prompt: Which is the longest river in the United Kingdom?
questions.explanation: The River Severn, which flows through Wales and England, is the UK's longest river, just ahead of the Thames.

questions.prompt: Which river flows through London?
questions.explanation: The Thames flows through the middle of London on its way to the North Sea.

questions.prompt: Which mountain is the highest in the United Kingdom?
questions.explanation: Ben Nevis in Scotland is the highest mountain in the UK, standing 1,345 metres tall.

questions.prompt: Which sea lies between Great Britain and Ireland?
questions.explanation: The Irish Sea separates the island of Great Britain from the island of Ireland.

questions.prompt: Which narrow stretch of water separates England from France?
questions.explanation: The English Channel is the narrow sea between southern England and northern France.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a historic county in the south west of England, known for cream teas and a rugged coastline?
questions.explanation: Cornwall is England's most south westerly county, with a long coastline and its own Celtic history.

questions.prompt: Which English county is known as 'the Garden of England' because of its orchards and hop fields?
questions.explanation: Kent, in the south east, has long been called the Garden of England for its fruit orchards and hop farms.

questions.prompt: Which city grew rich as a port on the River Mersey and was once a major departure point for ships crossing the Atlantic?
questions.explanation: Liverpool sits on the River Mersey and was once one of the world's busiest ports for transatlantic voyages.

questions.prompt: Which city, in the north east of England, takes its name from the river it sits beside?
questions.explanation: Newcastle upon Tyne is named after the River Tyne, which runs through it.

questions.prompt: Which people built long, straight roads across Britain and founded the settlement that became London?
questions.explanation: The Romans occupied much of Britain from AD 43, building roads, walls and towns including Londinium.

questions.prompt: In 1066, which battle saw William of Normandy defeat King Harold and become King of England?
questions.explanation: William, Duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, beginning Norman rule of England.

questions.prompt: Which document, signed by King John in 1215, said that even the king had to obey the law?
questions.explanation: Magna Carta, meaning 'Great Charter' in Latin, was signed in 1215 and is seen as an early step towards the rule of law.

questions.prompt: Which Tudor king had six wives and broke from the Catholic Church to found the Church of England?
questions.explanation: Henry VIII married six times and split from Rome in the 1530s, becoming head of the new Church of England.

questions.prompt: Which Tudor queen ruled England for 45 years and gave her name to an era of exploration and theatre?
questions.explanation: Elizabeth I reigned from 1558 to 1603, a period known as the Elizabethan age, famous for explorers and playwrights like Shakespeare.

questions.prompt: The Domesday Book, an enormous survey of land and property in England, was ordered by which king?
questions.explanation: William the Conqueror ordered the Domesday Book in 1086 to record who owned what land across England.

questions.prompt: The Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain in the 1700s, saw a huge shift towards making goods how?
choices: By trading with other countries only
questions.explanation: New machines and factories, often powered by steam, changed how goods were made and where people worked.

questions.prompt: Which fuel powered the steam engines that drove Britain's Industrial Revolution?
questions.explanation: Coal, mined in huge quantities, fuelled the steam engines that powered Britain's factories, trains and ships.

questions.prompt: The First World War began in 1914. In which year did it end?
questions.explanation: The First World War ran from 1914 to 1918, ending with an armistice on 11 November.

questions.prompt: During the Second World War, thousands of British children were sent from cities to the countryside for safety. What was this called?
questions.explanation: Evacuation moved children out of cities that were likely to be bombed and into safer homes in the countryside.

questions.prompt: The Battle of Britain in 1940 was fought mainly by which part of the armed forces?
questions.explanation: RAF pilots fought off German bombers and fighters in the skies over southern England in 1940.

questions.prompt: Which Roman structure, built across the north of England, marked the edge of the Roman Empire?
questions.explanation: Hadrian's Wall was built by the Romans in the AD 120s to mark and defend the northern edge of their province of Britannia.

questions.prompt: During and after the Second World War, what did British families need to buy scarce foods like sugar, meat and butter?
questions.explanation: Ration books gave each person a fair share of scarce food and other goods during and after the war.

questions.prompt: In 2022, after the death of Queen Elizabeth II, who became King?
questions.explanation: Charles III became King in September 2022, after his mother Elizabeth II had reigned for 70 years.

questions.prompt: Which 1381 uprising saw peasants march on London to protest against an unfair tax?
questions.explanation: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 was led by Wat Tyler and was one of the biggest uprisings in medieval English history.

questions.prompt: The Glorious Revolution of 1688 replaced King James II with which joint monarchs?
questions.explanation: In 1688, Parliament invited William of Orange and his wife Mary to become joint monarchs instead of James II, strengthening Parliament's power.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the UK Parliament's elected house?
questions.explanation: The House of Commons is made up of MPs elected by voters across the UK.

questions.prompt: What does MP stand for?
questions.explanation: MPs are Members of Parliament, each elected to represent one local area, called a constituency.

questions.prompt: Who usually becomes Prime Minister?
choices: The leader of the party with the most MPs
questions.explanation: The Prime Minister is normally the leader of whichever party can command the most support in the House of Commons.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the UK Parliament's other house, whose members are not elected by the public?
questions.explanation: Members of the House of Lords are appointed or, in a few cases, inherit their seat, rather than being elected.

questions.prompt: At which London address does the Prime Minister live and work?
questions.explanation: 10 Downing Street has been the Prime Minister's official home and office for centuries.

questions.prompt: At least how often must a general election be held in the UK, by law?
questions.explanation: UK law requires a general election at least every five years, though one can be called earlier.

questions.prompt: Before a new law can take effect, who must give final approval once both Houses of Parliament agree it?
questions.explanation: Once both Houses agree a bill, it becomes law only after the monarch gives royal assent, a formality that has not been refused in centuries.

questions.prompt: What is the building where the UK Parliament meets commonly called?
questions.explanation: Parliament meets in the Palace of Westminster, beside the River Thames, whose clock tower holds the bell known as Big Ben.

questions.prompt: Which MP is chosen to keep order in the House of Commons and decide who gets to speak?
questions.explanation: The Speaker of the House of Commons runs debates, decides who speaks and stays neutral between parties.

questions.prompt: What is the name for an MP whose job includes making sure their party's MPs turn up and vote as the party wants?
questions.explanation: Whips organise MPs and try to make sure they turn up and vote with their party.

questions.prompt: Roald Dahl, who wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and Matilda, wrote mostly for which audience?
questions.explanation: Roald Dahl was one of Britain's best loved children's authors, known for imaginative and often mischievous stories.

questions.prompt: William Shakespeare, one of the most famous writers in English, mainly wrote what?
questions.explanation: Shakespeare wrote plays such as Romeo and Juliet and Macbeth, plus many poems called sonnets.

questions.prompt: In which English town was William Shakespeare born?
questions.explanation: Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564, and the town still celebrates his life and work.

questions.prompt: Charles Dickens often wrote about poverty and hardship during which era of British history?
questions.explanation: Dickens wrote during the 1800s, the Victorian era, and often described the harsh lives of poor children in cities.

questions.prompt: In Charles Dickens' story A Christmas Carol, which character is visited by three ghosts?
questions.explanation: Scrooge, a miserly old man, is visited by the ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Yet to Come, and changes his ways.

questions.prompt: The theatre where many of Shakespeare's plays were first performed, on the south bank of the River Thames, was called what?
questions.explanation: The Globe Theatre, built in 1599, staged many of Shakespeare's plays. A replica now stands near the original site in London.

questions.prompt: In the metric system used across science and most of the world, what is the standard unit of length?
questions.explanation: The metre is the base unit of length in the metric system, used in science and in most countries' everyday measurements.

questions.prompt: What is the standard SI unit of mass?
questions.explanation: The kilogram is the base SI unit of mass, used for everything from a bag of sugar to a person's weight.

questions.prompt: In the SI system, at what temperature does water freeze, in degrees Celsius?
questions.explanation: Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius and boils at 100 degrees Celsius under normal pressure.

questions.prompt: Even though the UK uses metric units for most things, which units does it still commonly use for road distances and speed?
questions.explanation: The UK measures most things in metric units, but road signs still show distances in miles and speeds in miles per hour.
